summary: New Zealand's smallest national park: golden beaches, granite headlands, clear estuaries and regenerating coastal forest at the top of the South Island. Most people walk or kayak the Abel Tasman Coast Track, a Great Walk of three to five days, and ride a water taxi one way. Fur seals bask on the headlands and little penguins nest on the islands offshore.
story: The park is built on Separation Point Granite, and the rock decides much of what you see: the golden sand of the beaches and stream beds, the sculpted headlands, and thin, infertile soils. Black beech covers the dry ridges near the sea, hard beech grows further inland, and lush forest of tree ferns, kiekie and supplejack fills the damp gullies. Sandy estuaries fill and empty with the tide twice a day, and they are easy to explore at low water.

Much of the land was milled, burned and farmed, and the forest is still coming back. Bellbird, fantail, pigeon and tūī are the main forest birds; Dumont d'Urville found South Island kōkako around Torrent Bay in 1827, but they and several other species have gone. Offshore, gannets, shags and terns dive for fish, little penguins return to burrows on the islands at night, and fur seals haul out on the remote headlands of Separation Point, Tonga Island and Pinnacle Island. Fourteen native fish species live in the park's streams.

Māori lived along this coast for at least 500 years, gathering food from the sea, estuaries and forest and growing kūmara where they could. On 18 December 1642 the Dutch navigator Abel Tasman anchored near Wainui in Mohua, Golden Bay, the first European visitor to New Zealand; four of his crew were killed in a clash with Ngāti Tūmatakōkiri, and he sailed on. Settlers arrived from about 1855, logging, building ships, stripping bark and quarrying granite at Tonga Quarry.

When more logging threatened the coast, Pérrine Moncrieff, who had made her own land near the Astrolabe Roadstead a private scenic reserve in 1936, led a campaign for a national park. It opened in 1942, the 300th anniversary of Tasman's visit, and has grown since. In 2016 a beachfront property at Awaroa, bought by the public through a crowdfunding campaign, became part of the park.
howItWorks: The park is run by the Department of Conservation (DOC). DOC says there are no fees to walk the Coast Track for the day or to enter the park; under the National Parks Act 1980 the public has freedom of entry and access. The park's boundary is the mean high water mark, so the beaches below it, the estuaries and the sea are outside the park, and Torrent Bay and Awaroa are private settlements surrounded by park land. The Tonga Island Marine Reserve, where all marine life is protected and fishing is banned, runs one nautical mile out from the coast between Awaroa Head and the headland between Bark Bay and Mosquito Bay.

The Abel Tasman Coast Track is one of DOC's Great Walks. Its 4 huts and 18 campsites must be booked in advance all year, for no more than two nights at each from October to April; freedom camping is not permitted, and campers may not use hut facilities. Great Walk huts are DOC's most comfortable, with mattresses, water, toilets and heating, but no meals; carry a stove, food and a sleeping bag. Most visitors walk one way and ride a commercial water taxi the other, between Mārahau or Kaiteriteri and Tōtaranui; there is no water taxi beyond Tōtaranui.

Dogs are not allowed in the park, on its islands or on the beach scenic reserve between Coquille Bay and Wainui, with a few exemptions next to private land. Tonga and Pinnacle islands, where seals breed, can be visited only with a permit; Adele and Fisherman islands can be landed on by boat or kayak, but have no toilets and no camping. Hammocks are not allowed in Coast Track campsites, and whitebaiting is no longer permitted in the park's streams. A free Abel Tasman visitor app, provided by Project Janszoon, works offline.

sights.name: Te Pukatea Bay
sights.note: A bay beside Anchorage with a Coast Track campsite, about four hours' walk from Mārahau.

sights.name: Cascade Falls
sights.note: A waterfall hidden in native bush, a steep 1 hour 30 minute return side trip on the Coast Track section from Anchorage to Bark Bay.

sights.name: Falls River suspension bridge
sights.note: A 47-metre suspension bridge over the inlet of Falls River, between Torrent Bay and Bark Bay.

sights.name: Onetahuti Bay
sights.note: One of the longest beaches in the park, reached after a climb through mānuka from Bark Bay and the old granite workings at Tonga Quarry.

sights.name: Tonga Island
sights.note: A specially protected island where fur seals breed, off Onetahuti Bay. Landing needs a permit.

sights.name: Awaroa Inlet
sights.note: A wide sandy estuary on the Coast Track that can be crossed only in daylight, from 1 hour 30 minutes before to 2 hours after low tide.

sights.name: Tōtaranui
sights.note: A beach and campsite at the northern end of the water-taxi service, with the historic Ngarata homestead; farmed until 1974.

sights.name: Separation Point / Te Matau
sights.note: The granite headland at the park's northern tip, where fur seals rest on the rocks and bryozoans build coral-like colonies under water.

sights.name: Motuareronui / Adele Island
sights.note: An island free of introduced mammal predators. Land by boat or kayak, check your gear for stowaway pests, and take everything away again.

entrances: Mārahau, the southern gateway, 67 kilometres from Nelson on sealed road — walking, kayaks and water taxis
Kaiteriteri, 61 kilometres from Nelson, for water taxis and kayaks
Tōtaranui, 32 kilometres from Tākaka, the last 12 kilometres unsealed but suitable for campervans
Wainui, the northern entrance, 21 kilometres from Tākaka
planYourVisit.reservations: Coast Track huts and campsites must be booked all year; bookings for 2026/27 are open. Check the tide tables before you book, since Awaroa Inlet can only be crossed near low tide, and check water-taxi times. Kayak hire, guided trips and water taxis are booked with local businesses.
permits: A permit to land on Tonga Island or Pinnacle Island
Mountain biking only on the Wainui–Gibbs Hill–Tōtaranui track, from 1 May to 30 September, in groups of up to eight
camping: Eighteen booked campsites along the Coast Track, among them Anchorage, Bark Bay, Onetahuti, Awaroa and Tōtaranui; tents only, no hammocks
Mosquito Bay campsite can be reached only by private boat or kayak
Tōtaranui campsite can be booked for one night only
lodging: Four Great Walk huts on the Coast Track: Anchorage, Bark Bay, Awaroa and the historic Whariwharangi, a homestead built around 1896
Accommodation in Mārahau, Kaiteriteri, Motueka and Tākaka
seasonalClosures: Hut and campsite stays are limited to two nights per site from 1 October to 30 April, and five from 1 May to 30 September

weather: The coast has a mild climate with sea breezes, dry summers and some winter frosts. DOC's management plan records rain on about 125 days a year, about 1,800 millimetres in all, and around 2,200 hours of sunshine. Summer days average 24°C with nights around 13°C; in winter the average high is 12.5°C and the low 4°C. From late spring through summer strong westerlies blow along the coast, while autumn and winter are generally calm. The inland Pikikiruna Range is cooler and wetter, with winter snow.
directions: The park sits at the top of the South Island, and the nearest towns are Motueka, Tākaka and Kaiteriteri. Mārahau, at the southern end of the Coast Track, is about an hour and a half by road from Nelson; Tōtaranui, near the northern end, about two and a half hours, the last 12 kilometres unsealed. Regular and on-demand buses run to the park from Nelson and the local towns, and water taxis and launches run along the coast between Mārahau or Kaiteriteri and Tōtaranui. A road reaches Awaroa from Tākaka, but its last 12 kilometres are rough, unsealed and prone to flooding, and DOC does not recommend it.

fees.title: Coast Track Great Walk huts, 1 October to 30 April
fees.detail: Per adult per night. Children: $28 for New Zealanders aged 5–17, $42 for international visitors aged 0–17; infants free. Proof of eligibility is needed for the New Zealand rate.

fees.title: Coast Track huts, rest of the year
fees.detail: Per adult per night, the same for all visitors: $42 in May, June and September, $33 in July and August.

fees.title: Coast Track campsites
fees.detail: Per adult per night from 1 October to 30 April; $21 for everyone from May to September. As listed by DOC in November 2026 — check before you go.

fees.title: Park entry and day walks
fees.detail: DOC charges no fee to enter the park or to walk the Coast Track for the day.

chronology.text: Māori are living along the coast, mostly seasonally, with permanent settlements in the Awaroa estuary.
On 18 December Abel Tasman anchors near Wainui in Golden Bay; four of his crew die in a clash with Ngāti Tūmatakōkiri.
Dumont d'Urville visits the coast and records Māori settlements in several bays.
The first farm is established at Tōtaranui, as permanent European settlement begins.
Pérrine Moncrieff makes her land near the Astrolabe Roadstead a private scenic reserve and campaigns for a national park.
Abel Tasman National Park opens, 300 years after Tasman's visit.
Farming ends at Tōtaranui, inside the park.
The Abel Tasman Birdsong Trust is formed to bring birdsong back to the park's forests.
Beachfront land at Awaroa, bought by the public through crowdfunding, is added to the park in July.

safety: Awaroa Inlet can only be crossed in daylight and within 1 hour 30 minutes before and 2 hours after low tide; Torrent Bay and Bark Bay estuaries within about 2 hours of low tide, or by the all-tide tracks. Check the tide tables before you set out.
Giardia has been found in the park's water. Boil, treat or filter all water before drinking.
Sections of the track can be steep, rough and muddy. Carry warm and waterproof clothing, a stove and enough food, with extra for emergencies.
Follow the Land Safety Code from DOC and the NZ Mountain Safety Council: choose the right trip, understand the weather, pack warm clothes and extra food, share your plans, and look after each other.
regulations: No dogs in the park, on its islands or on the foreshore scenic reserve between Coquille Bay and Wainui, except where DOC's exemptions allow.
Coast Track huts and campsites must be booked for every night, and freedom camping is not permitted. No hammocks in campsites.
Tonga and Pinnacle islands are open only with a permit. No camping on Adele or Fisherman islands, and no fires there, including barbecues and beach fires.
No fishing in the Tonga Island Marine Reserve, and no whitebaiting in the park's rivers and streams from Taupō Point to Tinline Stream.
Mountain bikes only on the Wainui–Gibbs Hill–Tōtaranui track, 1 May to 30 September.
